title: Invariant complements for rational sl2 operators
statement: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbf Q$-vector space [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace] and let $E,F,H\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbf Q}(V)$ satisfy $HE-EH=2E$, $HF-FH=-2F$, and $EF-FE=H$. If $U\subseteq V$ is a $\mathbf Q$-linear subspace with $E(U)\subseteq U$, $F(U)\subseteq U$, and $H(U)\subseteq U$, then there is a $\mathbf Q$-linear subspace $C\subseteq V$ such that $V=U\oplus C$, $E(C)\subseteq C$, $F(C)\subseteq C$, and $H(C)\subseteq C$. Here $V=U\oplus C$ means that every $v\in V$ has a unique expression $v=u+c$ with $u\in U$ and $c\in C$. No faithfulness, nilpotence, diagonalizability, or algebraic-closure hypothesis is imposed. The cases $V=0$, $U=0$, $U=V$, and $E=F=H=0$ are included.

source.place: Theorem 23.70, proof (a), printed p.507: Weyl’s theorem that finite-dimensional representations of a semisimple Lie algebra over a characteristic-zero field are semisimple. Specialization to the rational Lie algebra of trace-zero 2 by 2 matrices with its standard e,f,h basis. This is the Weyl input invoked in the proof, not the group-integration conclusion of Theorem 23.70.

proof.text: Let $L=\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbf Q)$ be the trace-zero $2\times2$ matrices with commutator bracket [def-wf-lie-algebra]. Its basis is $e=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $f=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $h=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Multiplication gives $[h,e]=2e$, $[h,f]=-2f$, $[e,f]=h$, so $L$ is perfect. It is simple: any nonzero ideal $I$ is preserved by $\operatorname{ad}h$; putting $T=\operatorname{ad}h$, the projectors $T(T+2)/8$, $T(T-2)/8$, and $1-T^2/4$ isolate its $e,f,h$ components, respectively, hence isolate the nonzero components of any $ae+bf+ch\in I$. Thus $I$ contains one of $e,f,h$ up to nonzero scalar. Bracketing with the other basis vectors gives all three. Since $[L,L]=L\ne0$, $L$ is not solvable, and its only solvable ideal is zero. Thus it is semisimple in [def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra].

source.place: Theorem 23.70 proof (a), p.507; explicit rational rank-one matrix verification supporting its Weyl input.

proof.text: The three given identities make the linear map $\rho(e)=E$, $\rho(f)=F$, $\rho(h)=H$ a Lie representation: bracket preservation is bilinear, so checking these three pairs and the alternating diagonal pairs suffices. A subspace is $L$-invariant exactly when it is stable under $E,F,H$, since $e,f,h$ span $L$. By [lem-sfb-perfect-lie-hyperplane-criterion], it suffices to show that every simple invariant hyperplane $W$ in every finite-dimensional rational representation $M$ of this fixed $L$ has an invariant complement. The criterion is over $\mathbf Q$ itself and requires only the perfectness proved above.

source.place: Lemma 22.40, pp.476-477, Lie-module criterion; Theorem 23.70 proof (a), p.507.

proof.text: Fix such $M,W$ with representation $r$. If $r=0$, any basis of $W$ extended to $M$ supplies a stable complementary line. Otherwise $r$ is injective: its kernel is an ideal, since $r([x,y])=[r(x),r(y)]$, and simplicity of $L$ makes a proper kernel zero. Apply [lem-sfb-faithful-semisimple-trace-form] to this injective representation of the three-dimensional semisimple rational Lie algebra $L$. Its hypotheses are exactly characteristic zero and finite-dimensionality of $L,M$. We obtain the nondegenerate form $B(x,y)=\operatorname{Tr}_M(r(x)r(y))$. Choose any basis $x_1,x_2,x_3$ and its $B$-dual basis $x^1,x^2,x^3$, obtained by inverting the Gram matrix, and put $c=\sum_i r(x_i)r(x^i)$.

source.place: Section 22c, The Casimir operator, p.475; Proposition 22.41, p.477, adapted to the rational Lie representation.

proof.text:
Trace cyclicity [lem-pc-finite-dimensional-trace-cyclic] gives $B([z,x],y)+B(x,[z,y])=0$: expand the two brackets and move the first factor of $\operatorname{Tr}(r(z)r(x)r(y))$ to the end. Write $[z,x_i]=\sum_j a_{ji}x_j$. Duality then gives $[z,x^i]=-\sum_j a_{ij}x^j$, by pairing with each $x_j$. Consequently
$$[r(z),c]=\sum_{i,j}a_{ji}r(x_j)r(x^i)-\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}r(x_i)r(x^j)=0,$$
by exchanging $i,j$. Also the matrix definition of trace [def-weil-endomorphism-trace] gives $\operatorname{Tr}_M(c)=\sum_i B(x_i,x^i)=3$. Thus $c$ commutes with the $L$-action, without invoking a group integration theorem.

source.place: Section 22c, p.475, Casimir commutation and trace calculation, expanded in a dual basis.

proof.text: The one-dimensional space $M/W$ has scalar endomorphisms, whose commutators vanish. Since $L=[L,L]$, its induced action is zero; therefore $r(x)M\subseteq W$ for every $x$. Each $r(x)$ preserves $W$, so $c(M)\subseteq W$. In a basis adapted to $W$, the diagonal blocks of $c$ are $c|_W$ and zero, hence $\operatorname{Tr}_W(c|_W)=3\ne0$. In particular $c|_W\ne0$. Its kernel is invariant by the commutation identity above. Since $W$ is simple, that kernel is zero. An injective endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space is surjective (its matrix has full rank), so $a=c|_W$ has an inverse. This argument replaces the algebraically closed Schur-lemma step of Proposition 22.41.

source.place: Proposition 22.41, p.477; agent rational-field replacement of its scalar Schur step by kernel and rank.

proof.text: Define $p=a^{-1}c:M\to W$. Since $a$ commutes with $r(z)|_W$, multiplying $ar(z)=r(z)a$ by $a^{-1}$ on both sides shows that $a^{-1}$ does too. Thus $p$ is equivariant and $p|_W=1_W$. Its kernel $D$ is invariant, and $m=p(m)+(m-p(m))$ exhibits $M=W+D$. If $w\in W\cap D$, then $w=p(w)=0$, so the decomposition is unique. This verifies the hyperplane antecedent for every $M,W$. Apply [lem-sfb-perfect-lie-hyperplane-criterion] to the original $V,U$ and take its complement $C$. Its invariance gives all three required stability clauses. If $U=0$ take $C=V$, and if $U=V$ take $C=0$, covering $V=0$; for the zero action any linear complement works.

source.place: Lemma 22.40 and Proposition 22.41, pp.476-477, retraction and invariant kernel; application to Theorem 23.70 Weyl input.

proof_origin.place: Weyl input in Theorem 23.70(a), p.507; expanded using the Casimir and hyperplane route of Section 22c, pp.475-477. Rational kernel/rank argument avoids algebraic closure.
